episode_title: The Shogun Who Made Hurting a Dog a Crime: Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, the 'Dog Shogun'
youtube_title: Japan's 'Dog Shogun' Made Hurting a Dog a Crime. The Dogs Were Only Half the Story
youtube_description:
Edo, 1695: kennels for thousands of dogs are rising outside the city, and the shogun behind them will be mocked as the "Dog Shogun." His orders also reached much further than dogs, a part of the story the joke usually leaves out. If you had been charged to feed those dogs, would you have called him cruel or kind?

📰 Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former Tokyo foreign correspondent. His grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to one day of Japan's past at a time. He can watch and he can speak, but he can never change what happens. This time he files his dispatch from a ward gate in Edo and the dog enclosures at Nakano, late in 1695. What happened before and after that day he reads from the record.

A town officer kneels with his lantern over a straw basket by the gatepost, and a thin dog watches him. Before I tell you what he finds, you need the story everyone already knows.

scenes.narration: Say Dog Shogun and the story arrives fast: a ruler who put dogs above people. A later story claims that a priest named Ryuko told him he had no heir because of killing in a former life, and that a man born in the year of the dog should protect dogs. I can confirm one detail: 1646, the year of his birth, is a dog year. The rest I treat with real caution. The tale seems to come from a satire written after his death, and historians doubt it. I set it aside.

I add no judgment to that.

scenes.narration: I open the code every warrior lord lives under. Its first line, set down under the early Tokugawa, told them to devote themselves to letters and arms, the way of the bow and the horse. In 1683 Tsunayoshi has it rewritten to press learning, arms, loyalty, filial duty and proper manners. The bow and horse are gone from that line. The ban on retainers following a lord into death, announced under his brother, now sits in the code. The same year his young son Tokumatsu dies. I will return to that.

scenes.narration: From the middle of the 1680s, orders about living things keep arriving in the wards. I find historians disagreeing about which one comes first, because this is not one law but a long run of notices. Dogs are not to be beaten. Even strays are to be fed. Wards must keep track of their dogs, down to the colour of the coat. If one is hurt, someone may have to answer for it. I watch a woman at a well meet a sleeping dog in her path. She does not shoo it. She waits.

scenes.narration: I walk west of the city to Nakano, where carpenters are raising long fenced yards and roofed sheds on open farmland. This year the government starts moving stray dogs off Edo's streets into these enclosures, and I hear of others nearer town. Later accounts put the number here in the tens of thousands. I cannot count them. I do see sacks of rice and baskets of dried fish going in. Townspeople will be made to help pay for the dogs' upkeep, and they can hardly miss it.

scenes.narration: Back in town, an old rice dealer tells me his complaint in a low voice. He says his ward pays for dogs it will never see again, while food keeps getting dearer. A dog howls at his door half the night, and he will not even raise a broom, because he has heard what happened to a man two wards over. So he feeds it, he says, and he smiles. I ask whether he saw that punishment himself. He shakes his head. I write it down as hearsay.

scenes.narration: The cost does not stop at dog food. Temple building, some of it tied to the shogun's mother, Keishoin, and grand ceremonies strain the treasury. This very year, 1695, the official Ogiwara Shigehide reissues the coinage with less gold in it. I watch a money changer weigh a new coin against an old one and frown. Prices will climb. Whatever else I find today, I will not call this government cheap or gentle. The townsman's grievance is real, and I put it on the page first.

scenes.narration: The child is not alone in these orders. As I read them, inns and villages must tend a traveller who falls ill, and must not simply pass him on to the next place. Sick horses and cattle may not be abandoned, and even the treatment of prisoners draws attention. Historians differ over which orders belong under one name, so I count them with caution. Still, the same stream of rules that shelters the dog at the gatepost reaches the baby beside it. The joke I carried here has no room for both.

scenes.narration: Why does he issue them? I weigh the answers. Buddhist teaching against taking life. The Confucian duty of a kindly ruler. His mother's faith. Hope for an heir after Tokumatsu's death, a link some draw and others doubt. And a harder aim: some historians argue he is breaking a warrior habit in which cutting down a stray, or worse, could still pass for nerve. I cannot settle which weighs most. I think no single answer is enough, and I am wary of anyone who offers one.

scenes.narration: The same man can be severe, and I carry the record of what comes later. In 1701 Lord Asano draws his sword inside Edo Castle and wounds the official Kira. Tsunayoshi orders Asano to take his own life that very day, and Kira goes unpunished. In 1703 the shogunate orders the ronin who avenge Asano to die the same way. I do not call this mercy. Nor do I call it madness. I read a ruler who wants blades sheathed, though that reading is mine.

scenes.narration: My notes turn to the first month of 1709. Tsunayoshi dies at sixty-four by the Japanese count, reportedly of measles. His successor Ienobu, the nephew he adopted as heir in 1704, moves quickly. Most of the rules about dogs are lifted, and the great kennels are wound down. Later, an anonymous satire, the Sanno Gaiki, adds colour, including the priest and the dog year. Over time I see the surviving portrait close in around the animals. At the gate, the officer carries the child indoors. I know how this reign will be told, and I cannot tell him. I only close my notebook.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. So why do we remember only the dog? My answer has three parts, and none works alone. First, the dog rules are the ones people pay for and see: yards outside the city, rice for strays, a broom you dare not raise. A child taken in at a ward gate is a quiet event, remembered perhaps by one street. The burden is direct and visible. I think a grievance travels further than a kindness, especially when the grievance has four legs and barks all night.
